title: Greetings and Their Replies
description: Every Yemeni greeting comes with a fixed reply, and the reply is the lesson. Hear the twelve pairs a Sanaa doorstep runs through — peace, morning, how are you, welcome, goodbye — until the answer arrives before you think.
approach: GPA Phase 1 — receptive first; every greeting is heard with its reply before it is said. Pairs are always presented together so the reply is learned as one unit with the call.
unlock_condition: ≥9/12 on the final listen-and-tap quiz, plus one recorded greeting-and-reply pair
can_do: Greet someone and answer their greeting
Say good morning, good evening and goodbye
Ask how someone is and say you are fine

grammar.title: -ak or -ish: who you are talking to
grammar.explanation: Sanaa greetings change their ending for the person in front of you. Talking to a man, the ending is -ak: كيف حالك kayf ḥaalak. Talking to a woman, Sanaa uses -ish: كيف حالش kayf ḥaalish — this -ish is the sound that tells everyone you learned your Arabic in the highlands. In Aden and Taʿizz the woman's ending is -ik instead. You do not need to produce this yet, only to hear the difference.

examples.english: How are you? (to a woman, Sanaa)
What's new with you? (to a man)

culture.title: The reply is the lesson
culture.note: In Yemen no greeting is left hanging. السلام عليكم is answered word for word with وعليكم السلام, صباح الخير gets صباح النور, and كيف حالك is answered بخير الحمد لله before anything else is discussed. Sanaa men shake right hands and may touch cheeks or noses briefly if they are close; a woman greets a man with words unless she offers her hand first. Elders and strangers are addressed with the plural (كيف حالكم؟ حياكم الله) even when they are alone — it is respect, not confusion.

phrases.english: How are you? (plural, or respectful to one elder)

culture.title: Morning, Sanaa style
culture.note: Sanaa has a longer morning greeting you will hear from older people and in the old city: صبّحكم الله بالخير — 'may God give you a morning of goodness' — answered with صبّحكم الله بالنور. The short صباح الخير works everywhere, but recognising the long form means you will not freeze when a neighbour uses it. In the evening the same pattern gives مسّيكم الله بالخير.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The all-purpose hello, safe with anyone at any hour. Yemenis also say هلا and أهلا, and often double it: مرحبتين 'two hellos' as the reply.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two men in Sanaa dress raising a hand in greeting across a stone lane.
vocabulary.video_hint: Two people meeting; the greeting is the first thing said.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The greeting that opens every room, shop and phone call. Said on entering, never answered with anything but its fixed reply. The ع in عليكم is the sound to listen for.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man stepping through a doorway into a room, hand on his chest, people inside looking up.
vocabulary.video_hint: Anyone entering a room or opening a video; street-interview intros.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Automatic and obligatory. The two halves swap order; nothing else changes. Learn it as one breath so it comes out before you think.
vocabulary.image_scene: Seated people turning toward a doorway and answering together, hands raised slightly.

example.english: And upon you peace — come in

vocabulary.video_hint: The reply audible right after someone's سلام; door scenes.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Used from waking until lunch. The emphatic ص at the start is heavier than an English s. Sanaa elders stretch it to صبّحكم الله بالخير — same meaning, same reply pattern.
vocabulary.image_scene: Sunrise over Sanaa rooftops, a man on a doorstep with a tea glass waving to a neighbour.

example.english: Good morning, Hajj (respectful to an older man)

vocabulary.video_hint: Morning-routine vlogs; the first words on camera in the morning.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'A morning of light' — the fixed answer to صباح الخير. Notice the article: النور sounds in-nuur, the l melting into the n.
vocabulary.image_scene: The neighbour on the opposite doorstep smiling back, morning light on the wall between them.
vocabulary.video_hint: The reply audible right after صباح الخير.

vocabulary.teaching_note: From late afternoon on — which in Sanaa is when the qat session breaks up and people are out again. Reply: مساء النور. The long Sanaa form is مسّيكم الله بالخير.
vocabulary.image_scene: Dusk in an Old Sanaa lane, lamps lit in the tower-house windows, two friends greeting.
vocabulary.video_hint: Evening street scenes and comedy sketches set at night.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Yemen uses كيف, not the Gulf شلون or the Egyptian إزيك. To a woman Sanaa says كيف حالش — that -ish is the Sanaa signature. The shorter كيفك is also common.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two men shaking right hands on a pavement, one leaning in with a questioning smile.
vocabulary.video_hint: Street interviews: the interviewer's first question after the salaam.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The only expected answer to كيف حالك, whatever your day was like. Say it, then return the question. The double l in الله is held longer and darker than an English l.
vocabulary.image_scene: A smiling man with his right hand on his chest, nodding, in a sunny Sanaa lane.
vocabulary.video_hint: The reply audible right after كيف حالك in an interview or sketch.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The word that marks a Sanaani. Where the rest of Yemen answers زين or طيب, old Sanaa says ناهي — 'fine, all well'. Recognise it now; you will hear it constantly in the old city and in comedy sketches imitating Sanaa speech.
vocabulary.image_scene: An elderly Sanaa man in a shawl and janbiya nodding contentedly from a shop doorway.

example.english: How are you? — Fine, thank God

vocabulary.video_hint: Sanaa-flavoured sketches; older speakers answering كيف حالك.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'may God give you life' — what a host says as you arrive and what a shopkeeper says as you walk in. Plural حياكم الله to a group or an elder. أهلاً وسهلاً is also heard and is the safe reply when it is said to you.
vocabulary.image_scene: A host at an open door gesturing a guest inside with his right hand, warm light behind him.
vocabulary.video_hint: A guest arriving at a house or shop; the host's first words.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said by the person staying to the person leaving — 'go with safety'. The one leaving answers الله يسلمك. The article assimilates: السلامة sounds is-salaama, not il-.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man waving from a doorway as a friend walks away down a stone lane.
vocabulary.video_hint: Ends of vlogs and sketches; someone leaving a room or car.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'We'll see you' — the casual goodbye between friends, often followed by بخير or إن شاء الله. To a woman: نشوفش in Sanaa.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two young men bumping fists beside a parked car, one already half turned to go.
vocabulary.video_hint: Sign-offs at the end of vlogs; friends parting.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The second question after كيف حالك, and the one that shows you know Yemeni: ايش is the Yemeni 'what', never the Gulf شخبارك. The reply is the same بخير الحمد لله or a simple تمام.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two friends sitting on a low wall with tea glasses, one asking with raised eyebrows.
vocabulary.video_hint: Phone-call openers and street interviews after the first greeting.

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.english: All well, thank God. Have some tea

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.english: God keep you — see you tomorrow

sound_spotlight.explanation: ع is a squeeze deep in the throat that colours the vowel after it; ء is a clean stop, like the catch in 'uh-oh'. Sanaa keeps both clearly — hear عليكم against the Sanaa yes إي.
Breathy h from the throat, no rasp. كيف حالك is the phrase you will say most, so ح is where production starts.
The Sanaa 'your (f.)' ending. Heard only, not produced yet — but it is the highland fingerprint, so ears go on it now.

lesson_sequence.detail: A Sanaa doorstep at morning. One line of English: greetings here always come in pairs — you will learn both halves.
Six greeting-and-reply pairs play as tiny two-line scenes with illustration; Arabic large, audio auto-plays, no English yet.
The same pairs with English shown small underneath; tap either half to replay.
A greeting plays; two replies are shown as cards; tap the right one. Covers السلام / صباح / كيف حالك / مع السلامة.
All twelve items, audio only, four-image grid.
Record السلام عليكم then كيف حالك and hear yourself next to the native audio. Feedback on ع and ح only.
Words-learned counter rolls up. Nudge: greet the next Arabic speaker you meet with السلام عليكم and wait for the reply.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Next time you enter a room with an Arabic speaker, say السلام عليكم and listen for وعليكم السلام coming back.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen. The lowest-risk first production a learner can attempt.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask a Yemeni friend كيف حالك؟ and try to catch whether they answer بخير, زين, طيب or the Sanaa ناهي.
real_world_prompts.context: Follow-up notification. Trains the ear on the reply variants.

real_world_prompts.prompt: In your next tutor session, ask them to greet you as a man, then as a woman, and hear the -ak / -ish switch.
real_world_prompts.context: Tutor prompt. Receptive contrast of the Sanaa feminine ending.

video_needs.scene: Two people greeting each other at a door or on the street; the reply audible; street-interview intros where the interviewer opens with the salaam and كيف حالك.
